subject: wyvernMount
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: saddled wyvern mount with reins and saddlebags.
Style: World of Warcraft.
reasoning:
This is a substantial task - I need to build a complete TypeScript module for a saddled wyvern mount in WoW style, roughly 700-1100 lines, and I'll need to be careful with API correctness since I can't test it directly. I'm settling on the design: a wyvern with two hind legs and wings serving as forelimbs with clawed thumbs, standing in a rest pose with wings spread and a long tail.

Now I'm thinking about the WoW identity angle more carefully. WoW actually calls its "wind rider" mounts wyverns, but those are more like lion-bodied manticore creatures with bat wings, manes, and scorpion tails, rather than the classic two-legged dragon-wyvern. I'm weighing whether to go with the more recognizable WoW wind rider design (quadruped plus wings, more complex) versus the classic wyvern silhouette rendered with WoW's chunky, hand-painted, vibrant aesthetic.

I'm fleshing out the wyvern's face details, mane, scorpion tail, and bat wings, while staying mindful of the joint and part budget. For sizing, I'm planning horse-to-dragon proportions: roughly 1.4m shoulder height, 2m head height, and a body spanning about 1.8m with a sizable wingspan.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton coordinates with +Z forward and +X left, starting from a hips root joint and building a spine chain through to the chest, neck, and head, then working out how the scorpion tail curves up and over the back toward the stinger.

I'll build the tail as a chain of eight tapering joints with carapace plates along each segment and a curved stinger spike at the tip. For the legs, I'm planning lion-like forelegs with IK across shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, with the elbow bending backward and wrist forward for that feline posture.

The hind legs follow a digitigrade structure instead, with the knee bending forward and hock back, giving a bent, haunch-like stance similar to the front legs' proportions.

For the paws, I'm planning chunky flattened spheres as the base shape with small toe spheres and claws, sized and positioned so they rest right at floor level with minimal sinking into the ground.

Now I'm working out the wing structure — a bat-like armature with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints spreading sideways in a T-pose, then fanning three fingers outward from the wrist to define the wing's leading edge and span.

I need to connect membranes between adjacent finger chains and from the last finger back to the body flank, making sure each membrane edge runs root-to-tip in matching directions so the mesh stretches correctly.

the body, essentially retracing the arm's path back toward the shoulder before continuing along the flank, so edge B should route through points below the elbow and shoulder before reaching flankFront and flankBack — that way the membrane naturally fills the space under the arm rather than cutting a straight chord across it.

That edge B length is around 2.9 while finger3 is about 1.6, so the strips will skew and the membrane could end up as a fan shape that might self-cross. I'm considering splitting into two separate membranes instead—maybe an arm membrane plus a flank membrane—or reworking which edges pair with finger3, looking at the wing from a top-down view to get the geometry right.

For the trailing edge near the body, I'll just let it default to the body bone rather than forcing a rigid assignment — edge B as a straight line from flank to finger3 tip should work fine as the trailing edge where the scallop pulls.

Actually, rethinking which edges get scallop here: scallop is meant for the membrane between two fingers where the trailing edge connects two tips, but for my inner quad the t=1 edge is wrist-to-finger3tip, which is the finger itself, not a webbing gap. So I shouldn't apply scallop there — instead I'll bow that trailing edge inward manually using a catmull curve with a midpoint pulled toward the body.

For the outer membranes, I'll apply scallop of 0.15 to the gaps between finger1-finger2 and finger2-finger3, since those are proper inter-finger webs. The leading edge (forearm into finger1) stays as the structural spar rather than a scalloped membrane, matching real bat wing anatomy. Now I'm laying out the skeleton as joint chains per side — shoulder, elbow, wrist, then each finger as two joints off the wrist.

Total joint count per side is shoulder+elbow+wrist(3) plus three fingers at two joints each(6) plus thumb(1) = 10, so 20 across both wings, with a clawed thumb spike jutting forward at the wrist.

For the membrane texture, I want tan/beige leather coloring with a dark-to-tan gradient from root to tip, mottled spotting, and simple vein lines for a tattered wyvern-wing look. Then for the head, I'm aiming for that classic WoW wyvern design — broad rounded skull, wide flattened snout, heavy lower jaw with tusks, small brow-shadowed eyes, and small horns.

Now I'm adding curved horns, pointed ears, a flowing mane around the neck and head, and a beard tuft under the chin, with amber slit-pupil eyes rendered as a decal on the skull surface rather than a separate textured sphere. I'm structuring the head as a scaled sphere skull with a forward snout loft, plus a separately jointed lower jaw that moves independently.

For the nose, I'm using a wide box with nostril cutouts, small downward-pointing cone teeth along the upper jaw, and upward tusks from the lower jaw. I'm working out that `head.local` directions refer to fixed model-space axes rather than the head's own tilted orientation, which keeps placement simple but means parts won't automatically follow if the head tilts -- something I'll just account for by keeping the head mostly aligned.

Instead I'll build everything directly in model space relative to a head center point, with a helper that scales offsets by a size factor to place parts. Roughly sketching proportions: head top near 2.3m, wingtips around 2.1m, body spanning about 4.4m nose to tail, and a wingspan near 6m -- reasonable scale for the creature.

Checking placements: rider saddle sits on the spine near the chest, resting just above the body's top surface given the torso radius; legs attach near the shoulder and hang down about a meter to the belly line. Wing roots at the shoulders need to align with the body's top-side surface at the chest cross-section, so I'm working out the x-offset where that surface sits.

The saddle needs to sit behind the wing roots, over the mid-back, so I'm placing its center further back along the spine. For the body itself, I'm planning a continuous loft along the spine with stations from the tail through hips, chest, and neck, each tied to bones so the mesh deforms with the skeleton, rather than treating the neck as a separate piece.

I'm setting up the skeleton now: hips as the root joint near the rump, then a spine chain running through catmull-interpolated points up toward the chest, broken into named spans so each segment of the body loft can bind to the right bone.

For the neck I'm using a two-span path up to the head joint, with the head angled slightly down and forward off the last neck joint. Then I'm adding a jaw joint hinged behind the head, and starting the tail chain branching off the hips.

I'm now figuring out limb parenting: front legs attach near spine3/chest, hind legs to hips, wings off chest, and saddle props rigid on spine2. For reins, I'm thinking through how to route them from the bit at the mouth down to the saddle horn, since they need to cross between separate bone chains.

Head has a jaw child so projection should still work fine. Now for the mane, the signature feature — I'm picturing the WoW wind rider's big crest of hair running from forehead down the neck, plus a shaggy collar, built from solid silhouette loft shapes along the neck top plus extruded blade cards for the shaggy texture. I'll place tapered flame-like mane blades along the dorsal neck line in mirrored angled pairs, painted with a root-to-tip gradient, supplemented by scattered cards for extra shagginess.

I'm working out the full color palette now: tawny tan fur with a lighter belly tone, a deep red-brown to rust to orange gradient for the mane, beige wing membrane with darker veins, bone-colored horns fading to dark tips, and dark brown tail carapace plates.

For the Horde-themed gear I'm planning dark leather saddle tones with cream stitching, red cloth with black trim and a generic tribal-style emblem (avoiding any trademarked symbol), plus dark iron studs with gold buckles. I'm also sketching out the texture list -- eye detail, emblem banner, zigzag saddle blanket trim, and possibly a flank brand -- aiming for around five to twelve total textures.

Now I'm working through how to apply the blanket texture onto the curved body surface using projected decals from the side rather than a flat top-down projection, since draping cloth over a round form needs careful UV handling.

I'm also sketching out the remaining texture cards: mane locks, fur tufts for cheeks and fetlocks, the tooled leather saddlebag flap reusing the emblem design, and considering whether to add a small glowing totem charm hanging from the saddle to bring in that lantern-and-magic feel the brief calls for.

Settling on just one glow effect to keep things restrained — a rune-carved medallion on the brow band of the bridle instead of scattering magic elements everywhere. For the wing membranes, I'm weighing whether to project tribal paint as a decal onto both faces or just paint the stripes directly onto the membrane surface, and leaning toward the paint approach since decals are tricky across double-sided geometry. I'm also considering adding similar tribal war-paint stripes to the face, departing a bit from traditional wyvern designs for extra stylization.

Setting up the imports now, pulling in the core builder utilities plus the glow kit for the rune medallion and the clockwork kit's metal paint for iron and gold fittings on the tack — checking whether these kit submodules import correctly and whether the rune would work better as a flat paint texture versus a glow effect.

I realize `mix` only accepts strings or Rgb values, not Paint objects, so I'll compose colors as raw hex strings inside the paint functions. Now I'm defining the fur paint, blending tawny and golden tones with layered noise for mottling and back-stripe darkening, plus belly cream and mud-darkened feet based on vertical position...

Still blending colors...

For wing membranes I'm thinking of veins as wavy lines at fixed fractional positions across the span, with darkening near the trailing edge for a tribal-style pattern.

Finishing the paint function with a cool backlit tint on the underside, then thinking about adding a Horde-style red war-paint chevron near the wing root as a tribal detail, and considering default membrane thickness settings.

Now I'm lofting the dragon's body, defining stations from rump to chest with width, height, and y-position values at each z-point to shape the torso profile before transitioning into the neck.

I'm weighing whether to include the tail chain in the body loft's bone list so the rump deforms naturally when the tail lifts, versus keeping it simple with just the spine bones.

Actually, I'll settle on [spine, neck] since hips and spine1 coincide and chest already owns the chest-to-neck1 span. For the neck sweep, I'm checking that its tapering radii bury properly into the body where it starts near the chest.

I need to extend the neck sweep slightly so it meets the head rather than leaving a gap, since the head joint sits just beyond the neck chain's end. I'm placing the skull's center a bit forward of the head joint itself, roughly at [0, 2.0, 1.46], to work out the head's sphere geometry.

Now I'm shaping the cranium as a scaled sphere, then adding brow ridges as angled capsules above the eyes to give the mount a fierce, heavy-browed look, with the left brow slanting from outer-upper to inner-lower.

Next I'm lofting the jaw forward through narrowing stations to form the snout, adding a flattened nose pad with dark nostril spheres, placing conical teeth and prominent canine fangs along the upper jaw's edge, and starting the lower jawbone loft from the hinge point.

Then I'm adding upward-pointing lower teeth, curved outward tusks sweeping from the jaw's front corners, and a chin tuft hanging beneath. For the eyes, I'm working out their placement on the cranium surface using the ellipsoid equation so they clear the snout's elliptical cross-section — checking that the snout's height falls off enough at the eye's x-position to avoid occlusion, and nudging the eye height upward slightly to stay clear.

I'm settling on a decal-based eye approach projected onto the cranium only, so the snout doesn't interfere, with brow capsules positioned safely above the eye's top edge. I'm deciding to keep the eyes non-glowing, styled as an almond shape with an amber iris, slit pupil, and dark outline, mirrored for the opposite side.

Now I'm working out the ears: pointed, tufted, placed behind the eyes near the top sides and angled back and outward, built from an extruded leaf-shaped outline with a sharp tip. I'm figuring out the right direction vectors so the extrusion length follows the ear's up-out-back angle while the cross-axis stays roughly perpendicular to it.

For horns, I'm thinking wyverns sometimes have small curved horns above the head, so I'll add a couple of short ones.

Now I'm working out the mane along the neck, placing flame-shaped blades that sweep backward from the dorsal line plus mirrored side blades angled off-center, computing the neck tube's surface points and tangents manually since the built-in sweep helper only covers the dorsal angle.

Checking the shape is non-intersecting, then building a local coordinate frame for the extrusion by orthogonalizing the back-direction against the surface normal. Now I'm thinking through proportions — blades should grow larger near the shoulders and crown, with a forelock tuft between the ears and flared cheek ruffs for personality. I also want scattered mane cards along the neck tube to add extra shagginess and volume.

For the overall mane silhouette, I'm considering a thick swept shape along the neck's top edge, offset outward from the chain's normal direction to build up the base mass.

Working out the shift direction for the mane mass sweep, I want it tilted toward the top-back of the neck, then I'll scatter the hair blades across that mass's own surface rather than the neck tube directly. Adding segment bulges toward the tip, then thinking through transitioning the tail colors from a furred base into chitin plates near the stinger using banded color regions.

I'm settling on default row/column counts for the membrane mesh.

Wyverns don't have claws at the finger tips, but a hooked thumb claw spike at the wrist makes sense, so I'm adding that as a rigid spike rather than a jointed chain. Tallying joints: each wing comes to 9 per side (6 finger joints, 3 arm, plus the thumb spike), bringing the full-body total to 54 joints across hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, tail, legs, wings, and ears. For the saddle placement, I'm computing the body's top surface height from spine2's position and half-height to get where it should sit.

Reconsidering the attachment entirely: maybe I should shift the saddle back further over the hindquarters, closer to WoW-style wyvern saddles, and shorten the wing's root span so the membrane attaches only near the shoulder rather than running the whole flank, adjusting coordinates for both the wing root and new saddle bounds.
